items.why: Clearly distinguishes his reason for leaving from the house he happens to reach.
Calls a conditional wish a request and mainly tests sentence order.
Requires identifying the mother as the speaker of the reported curse, rather than the current quotation.
Clearly tests Micah’s stated reason for expecting divine favor.
Tests the meaningful distinction between the relatives carrying the message and its intended audience.
The reported field outing and people coming out describe nearly the same event, weakening the contrast.
The sender is unambiguous, but identifying him requires little beyond direct retrieval.
Distinguishes his specific intention to burn the tower from the attack already underway.
The vague phrases 'do something' and 'the report' obscure what the question is asking.
Requires understanding the rhetorical question as reluctance to give up valuable oil.
The shadows-versus-people contrast is clear, but the question’s unexplained 'they' is awkward.
Clearly asks about the mother’s stated plan rather than who later performs the work.
Requires linking the burning of the occupied stronghold to the people’s deaths.
Readers can infer the refusal from the tree’s unwillingness to sacrifice its sweet fruit.
Distinguishes the priests’ endpoint from the idol’s, though 'captivity of the land' is opaque.
Assumes a later event, although the curse describes the punishment rather than something happening afterward.
His fear of Abimelek clearly explains why he escapes and lives elsewhere.
The roundabout description of Micah’s house makes an already awkward region-versus-destination sequence harder to follow.
Requires connecting the servant’s victim with Abimelek, who is named in the final sentence.
Clearly distinguishes the five men’s initial taking from the priest’s later taking of the same objects.
Shouting is the immediate cue, though being overtaken also contributes to the encounter.
Following 'him' back to Jerub-Baal yields a clear answer without outside knowledge.
Clearly separates the cause of prosperity from the comparison describing their safety.
Tests how distance and lack of outside ties explain the absence of rescuers.
Distinguishes the priest asked to inquire from God, whom he is to consult.
Clearly separates the five men entering the house from the priest and soldiers remaining outside.

The land is the intended answer, but taking over its people is not cleanly excluded.
Tests the stated reason for seeking land rather than mistaking the opening background for the cause.
The speakers make 'our' clear, though 'whose ruler' is an awkward way to ask.
Clearly distinguishes cursing during the feast from the earlier work with the grapes.
